organizations.name: ISKP
organizations.notes: Claimed the Aug 2020 Jalalabad prison attack. Afghan officials accuse the Haqqani Network of using it as a cutout. The hosts favor a 'tactical accommodation' theory. It has recruited Taliban and Haqqani defectors.

organizations.name: Islamic State
organizations.notes: Lost its territorial caliphate but remains a global insurgency. Its central media apparatus claimed the Jalalabad raid.

organizations.name: Taliban
organizations.notes: Signed US withdrawal deal in Doha on 29 Feb 2020. Rejected the ISIS caliphate. Officially denies al-Qaeda presence in Afghanistan.

organizations.name: Haqqani Network
organizations.notes: Integral to the Taliban. Historic al-Qaeda host and ally. Proxy of Pakistan's ISI. Core of the Kabul attack network. Designated a terrorist organization around 2012.

organizations.name: al-Qaeda
organizations.notes: Mansour accepted Zawahiri's oath. Sheltered by the Haqqanis in 2001-02 and in North and South Waziristan.

organizations.name: Kabul attack network
organizations.notes: Term coined by the US military around 2010. The Haqqanis were its spearhead, with leaders drawn from them. It supplied safe houses, logistics and expertise for attacks in Kabul.

organizations.name: Islamic Movement of Uzbekistan
organizations.notes: Part of the Kabul attack network.

organizations.name: Hezb-e-Islami Gulbuddin
organizations.notes: Once part of the Kabul attack network; its leader later joined the government.

organizations.name: UN Monitoring Team
organizations.notes: Its May 2020 report cites communication intercepts tying ISKP-claimed attacks to known Haqqani network members and describes a 'tactical accommodation'.

organizations.name: Afghan government

events.description: ISIS-K assault on Jalalabad prison: SVBIED rammed the gates and two ISIS teams infiltrated, causing a roughly 20-hour siege into 3 Aug. At least 29 were killed and hundreds of prisoners escaped.
Andarabi claims the new ISKP leader is Haqqani and that a local Taliban commander was behind the Jalalabad jailbreak.
US-Taliban withdrawal deal signed in Doha.
New York Times publishes an op-ed attributed to Sirajuddin Haqqani that blames the US for the war and does not name al-Qaeda.
UN Monitoring Team report finds ISKP-claimed attacks traceable via intercepts to known Haqqani network members and cites a 'tactical accommodation'.
Ten young ISIS-K gunmen assaulted the Afghan Interior Ministry offices in Kabul after Gen. Nicholson blamed the Taliban/Haqqanis. ISIS then claimed the attack with a photo and video.
Mullah Mansour killed after rejecting the ISIS caliphate and praising bin Laden and Zawahiri.
Hibatullah Akhundzada statement that Mattis described as a Taliban peace plan.
Boston bombing, cited as inspired by Khorasan mythology.
Trump, asked about Russian bounties on Americans, says the US also supplied weapons to those fighting the Russians.
Bin Laden fled to Sudan while keeping in contact with Jalaluddin Haqqani.
US designated the Haqqani Network as a terrorist organization (hosts say around 2011-2012).
Jalaluddin and Sirajuddin Haqqani sheltered fleeing Taliban and al-Qaeda during the 2001-02 US invasion.
Jalaluddin and Sirajuddin Haqqani sheltered al-Qaeda and Taliban fleeing the US invasion.
Iran and the Taliban nearly went to war after the Taliban killed Iranians in Mazar-i-Sharif.
Times Square bombing plot overseen by Hakimullah Mehsud.
Treasury designated the IRGC Ansar Corps for supporting the Taliban.
Afghan Black Hawk helicopter downed by an anti-tank missile in Helmand.
Afghan Black Hawk helicopter downed by an anti-tank missile during an evacuation mission in Helmand.
The New York Times reported that Iran is suspected of supplying the missiles.
Attack on Forward Operating Base Chapman, facilitated by Haqqani territory and carried out by a double agent.

key_claims: Afghan officials claim ISKP acts as a cutout for the Haqqani Network; the hosts consider this possible but unproven and lean toward a milder 'tactical accommodation' or facilitation.
The cutout theory ignores ISKP's own agency, its independent Nangarhar network and its central media arm, which claimed the Jalalabad and 2018 Kabul attacks with foreknowledge.
The Taliban and Haqqanis would risk undercutting their dominance of the jihad if they backed ISIS, a rival that rejected the Taliban emirate.
ISKP recruits defectors from the Taliban and Haqqanis, which could explain biometric links to former Haqqani fighters and the group's tactical know-how.

The Haqqani-led Kabul attack network (with the Taliban, al-Qaeda, IMU and HIG elements) supplied the infrastructure and expertise for Kabul attacks, so Haqqani fingerprints on some ISKP attacks are plausible.

Jalaluddin and Sirajuddin Haqqani were bin Laden's longtime hosts and shelterers, and the US never fully reckoned with the Haqqani-al-Qaeda relationship; the 9/11 Commission report never mentions the Haqqanis.
The Feb 2020 Sirajuddin Haqqani op-ed was likely ghostwritten disinformation: it never named al-Qaeda and blamed the US for the war.
The Taliban's official position is that al-Qaeda is not in Afghanistan, and Mansour had accepted Zawahiri's oath.
The Haqqani Network has been a core of local, regional and global jihad, sheltering al-Qaeda from the 1990s onward.
About 40% of Pakistan drone strikes hit Haqqani-controlled territory, often killing al-Qaeda leaders alongside Haqqani members.
The Haqqanis are backed by the Pakistani state, which the hosts argue should be designated a state sponsor of terrorism.
The Haqqani Network facilitated the Camp Chapman attack by giving the TTP a pass-through.
The Taliban relaunched their insurgency from Waziristan, driven largely by the Haqqanis, who were sheltering al-Qaeda.
Iran is suspected of supplying anti-tank missiles used to down Afghan Black Hawks, though no evidence has been released.
The Iran-Taliban relationship runs back to 2000-2001 through Kerkwa, and is documented in designations across three US administrations.
